organ transplantation

Slide 1
  • Dr. Abdullah M. Aloraini M.B.B.S, MPH, FRCSC
  • Consultant Hepatopancreatobiliary and Transplant Surgery

Introduction

Slide 2
  • Definition:
    • Transplantation is the process of transferring an organ, tissue, or cell from one place to another. An organ transplant is a surgical procedure in which a failing organ is replaced by a functioning one.
    • The organ is transplanted either Orthotopically or Heterotopically.
Notes

Definition & Basic Concepts

DEFINITION
Transplantation = transfer of an organ, tissue, or cell from one site/person to another; a failing organ is replaced by a functioning graft.
ORTHOTOPIC
Graft placed in its normal anatomical location (e.g. liver).
HETEROTOPIC
Graft placed at a different anatomical site (e.g. kidney in the iliac fossa).

Tissue transplantation: cornea, skin, vessels, tendons, bone. Vascular grafts are relatively non-immunogenic (may be transplanted without irradiation); bone/tendon grafts can be irradiated and stored in tissue banks.

  • Transplants that need immunosuppression → liver, kidney, heart, small intestine (not cornea, tendon, skin, bone, heart valves). 437
Slide 3

History of transplantation

Slide 4
  • Transplantation can be found in old mythological tales of chimeric beings.
  • Myth of Sts Cosmas and Damian where they replaced leg of a roman man with recently deceased Ethiopian.
  • 1903-1905 : Alexis Carrel developed method of joining blood vessels, also worked on transplant within animals, won Nobel Prize in 1912 in Medicine.
  • 1914-1918 Skin grafting was used on victims and soldiers during WW I.
  • 1953 drs Medawar and Burent first understanding of transplant immunology and immunosuppression.
  • 1954 Dr. Joseph Murray first successful kidney transplant from Ronald Herrick to his identical twin, he survived 8 years afterwards.
Slide 5History of transplantation
  • 1958 HLA was described and used for tissue and organ matching.
  • 1962 first kidneys, liver and lung recovered from deceased donors
  • 1963 first organ recovered from brain dead donor.
  • 1966 first successful pancreas transplant by Kelly and Lillehei
  • 1967 first successful liver transplant by dr.Thomas Starzl
  • 1981: First successful heart/lung transplant by Dr. Reitz at Standford
  • 1983 First successful lung transplant by Dr. Joel Cooper
  • 1984 Congress passed the National Organ Transplant Act (NOTA) which stated that it was illegal to buy/sell organs,
  • 1983 Cyclosporin approved 1990 tacrolimus approved 1995 mycophenolate mofetil approved
  • 1999 pancreatic islet cell transplant by Dr. Shapiro
  • Excludes a cadaveric liver donor → active systemic bacterial infection 436 ×4; brain-dead 62-year-old wanting to donate → contraindicated by history of melanoma (age > 60 and steroids are not absolute). 436 ×2
  • Na 190 for 48 h in a brain-dead donor → keyed exclude kidney, pancreas and liver (severe hypernatraemia > 170 damages grafts). 436

Types of grafts

Slide 6
  • Autologus (Autogrfts):
    • Grafts transplanted from one part of the body to another in the same individual.
  • Syngeneic (Isografts):
    • Grafts transplanted between two genetically identical individuals of the same species.
  • Allogeneic ( Allografts):
    • Grafts transplanted between two genetically different individuals of the same species.
  • Xenogeneic (Xenografts):
    • Grafts transplanted between individuals of different species.
  • Kidney from an identical-twin sister → isograft. 438 ×10

Immunology

Slide 7
  • The Immune system is designed to defend the body from microorganisms, but also can recognise the transplanted cells as foreign. ( self and non-self)
  • Organ transplant without immunosuppression ===> Rejection !
  • The antigen-encoding genes are located on chromosome 6
  • Main antigen in this process is MHC, and they make up Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA).
  • Two types of HLA:
    • Class I antigens (HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C) are expressed by all nucleated cells.
    • Class II antigens (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, and HLA-DQ) are expressed by antigen presenting cells (APCs) such as B lymphocytes, dendritic cells, macrophages, and other phagocytic cells.
Notes

Transplant Immunology

Graft = non-self→Immune attack→Graft rejection→Needs immunosuppression
Slide 8Immunology
  • The principal function of HLA antigens is to present the fragments of foreign proteins to T lymphocytes.
    • Interaction can be direct or indirect.
  • Many TCR interaction and signalling could happen, and commonly need more than one mechanism.
  • Two well-characterized co-stimulatory interactions are the CD40/CD154
  • Antigen binding and costimulation leads to the activation and clonal expansion of T cells. T cells differentiate into helper (CD4-positive) and effector (CD8-positive) cells that are able to secrete cytokines and kill target cells.
Notes

HLA / MHC

BASICS
Major transplant antigen genes lie on chromosome 6. Human MHC = HLA. Main function: present foreign protein fragments to T lymphocytes → immune activation.
HLA ClassExpression
Class IMost nucleated cells
Class IIPrimarily antigen-presenting cells (lymphocytes/macrophages)
Donor-antigen recognition occurs via direct or indirect pathways with multiple costimulatory interactions — e.g. CD40–CD154. Understanding these pathways allows targeted immunosuppressive drugs.
REJECTION MECHANISM
Inflammation is central and can begin around transplantation. Interplay of T cells, B cells, APCs, cytokines, antibodies → inflammation + graft tissue damage.

Rejection

Slide 9
  • Inflammation lies at the heart of the rejection process and is activated through early events around the time of transplantation.
  • Rejection is due to a complex interaction of different components of the immune system, including B and T lymphocytes, APCs, and cytokines.
  • The end result is graft damage caused by inflammatory injury.
  • Types of Rejection
    • Hyperacute
    • Acute
    • Ahronic
Slide 10
  • Hyper-Acute:
    • rapid irreversible damage to the organ within the first hours of organ reperfusion.
    • It is triggered by preformed antibodies against the donor’s HLA or ABO blood group antigens
    • Primary humoral mediated.
    • Plasmapharesis vs IVIG
  • Acute:
    • most common type, but can be reversible in early phases.
    • can be cellular (T-cell) or humoral (Antibody) mediated rejection
    • happens days or weeks post transplant.
    • Diagnosed by organ biopsy in clinical suspected cases.
  • Chronic:
    • This usually occurs after 6 months and often leads to a progressive decline in, and eventually loss of, organ function.
    • Takes time, usually over years, and likely multifactorial.
    • Histologically it is characterized by cellular atrophy and fibrosis,
Notes

Types of Graft Rejection

FeatureHyperacuteAcuteChronic
TimingMinutes–hoursDays–weeks>6 months
MechanismPreformed recipient antibodies (prior sensitization) vs HLA/ABOT-cell mediated (most common) or antibody- mediatedGradual progressive decline in function
Key pointAntibody-mediated → aggressive, hard to suppressMost common; reversible if treated earlyHistology distinguishes from acute
ManagementDetect in pre-transplant matching; plasmapheresis + IVIGDiagnosis by graft biopsy—
WHY BIOPSY?
Deteriorating graft function may be rejection, infection, or intrinsic graft dysfunction — biopsy differentiates these.
  • Kidney recipient unstable (hyperthermia, tachycardia) in the recovery room/at closure with no arterial flow → hyperacute rejection — pre-existing antibodies against donor proteins. 436 ×2 437

Histocompatibility

Slide 11
  • Pre-Transplant compatibility testing includes:
    • ABO compatibility
    • HLA compatibility

Immunosuppression

Slide 12
  • Development of Cyclosporin in 1983 has made a marked increase in allograft survival.
  • Balance between the immune response, Immunosuppression side effect and viability of graft.
  • Immune response is largely medicated by T-cells.
  • Highest during the first few days, then first 6 months.
  • usually multi drug regimen, and divided into
    • Induction :with anti-T-lymphocyte–depleting or nondepleting antibodies
      • antithymycite (Thymoglobulin) vs Basiliximab
    • Maintenance:with calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferative agents, and corticosteroids.
  • Drug used for induction → antithymocyte globulin. 439
  • Lung recipient on prednisone + a drug that inhibits T-cell activation → cyclosporine 437 ×2; cyclosporine's mechanism → inhibits T-cell activation (calcineurin inhibitor → ↓ IL-2 transcription). 437 ×2
Notes

Compatibility & Immunosuppression

PRE-TRANSPLANT TESTING
ABO compatibility + HLA compatibility. Rejection risk is highest in the early post-transplant period, especially the first months.
THE BALANCE
Prevent rejection ⟷ drug toxicity · infection/malignancy risk · graft injury from immunosuppressive drugs.
INDUCTION
Given around the time of transplantation → strongly reduces early immune activation/rejection.
MAINTENANCE
Lifelong, usually combination — backbone = calcineurin inhibitor + another agent.
  • Absolute contraindication to kidney transplantation → active malignancy. 441 ×3
Slide 13

Immunosuppression complications

Slide 14
  • Infection: closely related to dose of meds.
    • Bacterial specially in the first month
    • Viral: including CMV ( latent in immunocompetent), HSV, EBV
    • Fungal
  • Malignancies:
    • SCC is 20 times higher in IS patients.
    • PTLD
    • B-cell Lymphoma ? EBV
    • Kaposi Sarcoma
  • Tell a patient on immunosuppression → ↑ squamous cell carcinoma (infection IS dose-related). 437
Notes

Complications of Immunosuppression

ComplicationDetails
InfectionCorrelates with intensity/dose. First month → bacterial; viral → especially CMV; fungal also occur
Malignancy↑ risk, including Kaposi sarcoma

Organ donation

Slide 15
  • Living donation
    • Kidney
    • Liver
  • Deceased donation
    • Donation after brain death (DBD)
    • Donation after circulatory death (DCD)
  • Heart-valve replacement from a circulatory-death donor → no immunosuppression needed. 439
  • Brain death declared by 3 consultants — the ICU calls the Saudi Center for Organ Transplantation (SCOT) (speaking to the family is also correct per old slides). 436 ×2
  • Colon cancer cured 20 years ago wanting to donate a kidney → keyed cannot donate (history of malignancy) 435; primary brain tumours (low-grade glioma, glioblastoma) are the exception — they can donate (rare extracranial spread). 435 435

Living donation

Slide 16
  • In some areas of the world, it is the main source
  • Advantages
    • Considered better grafts
    • Transplants are planned properly.
  • Disadvantages
    • Surgically challenging
    • Legal and Ethical concerns
    • Risks on the donor.

Deceased donation

Slide 17
  • Donation after circulatory death (DCD):
    • Donors have suffered a devastating injury with no chance of a meaningful recovery but do not meet the criteria for brain death.
    • Withdraw of care happens, and organs only retrieved after cardiac arrest.
    • Longer warm ischemic injury time.
    • Considered lower quality grafts
Notes

Organ Donation

FeatureLiving DonationDBDDCD
DonorHealthy person (kidney, liver)Brain death — irreversible loss of brainstem functionDevastating brain injury, not meeting brain- death criteria
Graft qualityHigher — donor extensively evaluatedGood; may be judged only at surgeryLower than DBD — warm ischemia

Key issueDonor morbidity/mortality; ethical/legal (no organ sales)Exclude reversible mimicsWarm ischemic time
from a healthy person.Donation After Circulatory Death (DCD)Living donation is a major source of transplants in the Middle East and parts of Asia; it is technically demanding because an organ/part is removed
No meaningful neuro recovery→Family elects withdrawal + donation→Death within organ-specific timeframe→Rapid retrieval ~10 min
MAJOR PROBLEM — WARM ISCHEMIA
Longer warm ischemic time → greater graft injury; retrieval must occur very rapidly after circulatory arrest.
Notes

Organ Retrieval & Preservation

Open chest/abdomen inspect organs·Expose aorta/IVC Cattell–Braasch·Cannulate aorta + IVC·Flush blood ice-cold solution + ice
PRESERVATION PRINCIPLE
Remove blood, replace with ice-cold preservation solution, surround with ice, keep warm ischemic time as short as possible — residual blood and warmth increase graft injury.
Slide 18Deceased donation
  • Donation after brain death (DBD):
    • Brain death is defined as the irreversible cessation of brain functions, including the brainstem.
      • Have to exclude conditions that may mimic the condition e.g drug overdose, hypothermia
      • Establish cause of neurological insult.
      • Clinical examination to to determine absence of brainstem reflexes.
      • Apnea test.
      • Ancillary testing e.g EEG, Angiography
      • Most countries require 2 physicians in 2 separate occasions.

Kidney transplantation

Slide 29
  • Optimal treatment for ESRD
    • Most common causes are Diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy.
  • It offers better quality of life, but also improves survival rates compared with patients on dialysis and is cost effective.
  • Pre-Operative Patient assessment include:
    • Malignancy
    • Infection
    • HLA and ABO matching
    • Cardiovascular assessment
      • Functional
      • Anatomical
    • Psychological and social.
  • True about liver transplant → 5-year survival > 75% (not heterotopic, no HLA matching). 437
Notes

Kidney Transplantation

OPTIMAL TREATMENT FOR ESRD
Common ESRD causes: diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy. Versus dialysis (several multi-hour sessions/week): better quality of life, improved survival, more cost-effective. ESRD patients are themselves relatively immunocompromised.
Notes

Pre-Transplant Assessment

EXCLUDE
Active malignancy
Active infection
PERFORM
ABO + HLA matching
Cardiovascular assessment
Psychological/social assessment
CARDIOVASCULAR ASSESSMENT — IMPORTANT
1. Functional: can the CV system tolerate major surgery? 2. Anatomical: are suitable vessels available? Severe arterial calcification may make transplant impossible — a calcified vessel may fracture when clamped → hemorrhage/limb ischemia → assess vessels before the OR.

Psychological/social evaluation ensures adherence to lifelong medication and adequate support.

Lengthen with a cuff of donor IVC — can nearly double venous length.

Pancreas Transplant

Slide 40
  • It is the only definitive treatment for type I DM.
    • Preferably patient with C-peptide deficiency.
    • ? studies on DM II and chronic pancreatitis.
  • Can be transplanted alone, or Simultaneous Pancreas-Kidney transplant (SPK)
  • Goals of transplants
    • Restore normal glucose homeostasis, and thus quality of life.
    • Halt progression and complications associated with DM.
    • Pancreas transplantation has been marked by the limitations of surgical complications, rejection, and scarcity of appropriate donors.
  • Similar Pre-op assessment to KTx
Notes

Pancreas Transplantation

ROLE
Restores endogenous insulin in type 1 diabetes — especially with renal failure. (Type 2 diabetes/chronic pancreatitis studied but not established routine indications.)
OPTIONS
Pancreas transplant alone
Simultaneous pancreas-kidney (SPK) — preferred when kidney also needed
GOALS
Normal glucose homeostasis
Better quality of life
Halt microvascular complications
DONOR LIMITATION
Numbers remain low — ideal donor is young, fit, low/normal BMI, free of pancreatic disease/diabetes; many deceased donors don't qualify.

Notes

Graft Preparation & Exocrine Drainage

Retrieved with spleen + duodenum, prepared on the back table. Part of the duodenum is preserved — supports blood supply/anatomical integrity and provides an outlet for exocrine secretions.

DrainageTechniqueConsequence
EntericDonor duodenum → recipient small bowelSecretions enter GI tract physiologically
BladderExtraperitoneal; donor duodenum → urinary bladderBicarbonate-rich secretions lost in urine → metabolic acidosis
Complications
• Bleeding · infection • Pancreatic leak •• • Metabolic acidosis (bladder drainage) •• Arterial/venous thrombosis • Graft pancreatitis • High risk of rejection
REJECTION — MAJOR CHALLENGE
Pancreas biopsy is hazardous; worsening glucose control suggests but doesn't prove rejection. In SPK, rejection often occurs in both → biopsy the kidney as a safer marker. Unmet need: a reliable serologic rejection test.
SEVERE GRAFT PANCREATITIS
Infected, leaking, bleeding or severely inflamed pancreas → major systemic illness; extreme cases → graft pancreatectomy.

Outcome: ~97% 3-year outcome/survival; in SPK the pancreas may reduce the rejection tendency of the kidney graft.

liver transplant

Slide 46
  • Large organ with numerous functions, including : metabolism, detoxification, synthesis, secretory, storage.
  • Slow deterioration of liver function could be without signs until liver failure.
  • When liver fails, it could effect the functions of other organs, leading to multi-system failure.
  • Indications:
    • Hepatcellular carcinoma.
    • Liver failure:
      • Primary.
      • Secondary
    • Most common indications are HCV and alcoholic cirrhosis.
    • Upcoming indication is fatty liver disease, Non-Alcoholic SteatoHepatitis (NASH).
Notes

Liver Transplantation

GENERAL PRINCIPLES
Liver performs metabolism + detoxification with major reserve → gradual deterioration may occur without obvious failure. Advanced failure affects other organs: hepatorenal syndrome (renal failure) and hepatopulmonary syndrome. HCC is an important indication in selected patients.
Slide 47liver transplant
  • New indications under research include: CRCLM, NETs, Hilar cholangiocarcinoma
    • Rule is if their expected survival > 50 % in 5 years.
  • Listing is based on Model for End stage Liver Disease (MELD score).
  • Pre-Operative Patient assessment include:
    • Malignancy
    • Infection
    • ABO matching
    • Cardiovascular assessment
      • Functional
      • Anatomical
    • Psychological and social.
      • Active alcohol or drug abuse.

MELD score takes in consideration:

Bilirubin

Serum Creatinine

Serum Na

INR

+/- Dialysis

Notes

Listing — MELD Score

MODEL FOR END-STAGE LIVER DISEASE
Prioritizes patients for transplantation using bilirubin, INR, creatinine (+ sodium in MELD-Na).
INTERPRETATION
Higher score = more severe disease / higher priority; candidates from the high teens upward; approaching 40 = very severe.
Notes

Exclude active malignancy (outside accepted indications)

• Psychological/social factors

Exclude active infection

CV system — functional + anatomical Ongoing alcohol/drug abuse; adherence

Acute liver failure

Slide 48
  • Drug related
  • Viral infection
  • Autoimmune/ Wilson’s disease.
  • Herbal related
  • Post-transplant
    • Hepatic Artery Thrombosis in the first week
    • Primary non-functioning.
  • Child C liver disease → liver transplant 426; 4-cm HCC with Child B → liver transplant (Milan) 438 ×5; autoimmune hepatitis (incomplete recall) → liver transplant. 435
Notes

Kidney vs Liver — Immunology

FeatureKidney / PancreasLiver
HLA matchingRequiredNot routinely required
ImmunogenicityHighly immunogenicRelatively less immunogenic
ABOCompatibleCompatible standard; ABO-incompatible possible in life-threatening cases with intensified immunosuppression
Combined graftsSPK: pancreas may protect kidneyLiver-kidney: reduces kidney rejection risk
Acute Liver Failure & Early Graft Failure
ConditionDetails
Acute liver failureDrug toxicity — paracetamol/acetaminophen; viral causes
Hepatic artery thrombosisMajor post-transplant vascular complication → acute graft failure
Primary nonfunctionNew liver fails without clear rejection; cause may remain uncertain → often urgent retransplantation
Anatomy & Anastomoses
VERY IMPORTANT
Liver transplantation is orthotopic and requires detailed knowledge of vascular and biliary anatomical variations. Cirrhotic liver: shrunken, coarse/nodular. Fatty donor liver: yellow, unhealthy → may be rejected.
ComponentReconstruction
1. Hepatic arteryArtery-to-artery
2. Portal veinVein-to-vein
3. Hepatic venous/IVC outflowCaval replacement or piggyback
4. Bile ductHealthy duct → duct-to-duct; unsuitable/diseased → hepaticojejunostomy
CAVAL REPLACEMENT
Donor liver retrieved with donor IVC; recipient IVC clamped above and below; diseased liver + IVC segment removed, donor IVC implanted.
PIGGYBACK
Recipient IVC preserved; donor hepatic venous outflow joined to recipient hepatic veins/IVC — essential in living-donor transplant (no donor IVC with a partial graft).
POLYCYSTIC LIVER DISEASE
Massive disease → liver failure, severe hepatomegaly, early satiety, major weight loss; may coexist with polycystic kidney disease (very large kidneys needing additional surgery).

Mastery Checklist

1 Orthotopic = normal position (liver); heterotopic = different site (kidney, extraperitoneal iliac fossa)
2 Autograft = same person; syngeneic = identical twin; allograft = same species (most common); xenograft = different species
3 1954 first successful kidney transplant (identical twins); 1967 liver (Starzl); 1983 cyclosporine transformed outcomes
4 HLA genes on chromosome 6: class I on most nucleated cells, class II on APCs; CD40–CD154 is a key costimulatory pair
5 Hyperacute = minutes–hours, preformed anti-HLA/ABO antibodies → plasmapheresis + IVIG
6 Acute = most common, days–weeks, mostly T-cell mediated, reversible if treated early — confirm with graft biopsy
7 Chronic rejection = >6 months, gradual decline in graft function
8 Induction around transplantation; lifelong maintenance built on a calcineurin inhibitor
9 Immunosuppression → infection (bacterial first month, CMV, fungal) + malignancy (Kaposi sarcoma)
10 Living donor grafts are higher quality and elective; DCD grafts are lower quality because of warm ischemia (~10 min retrieval)
11 Brain death: neurologic cause, exclude hypothermia/drugs, absent brainstem reflexes, 2 doctors at separate times
12 Kidney transplant work-up: exclude malignancy/infection, ABO + HLA, functional AND anatomical CV assessment (calcified vessels)
13 Kidney: extraperitoneal, iliac vessels, ureter to bladder dome; short right renal vein → IVC extension; Carrel patch
14 Kidney graft survival: living 98% (1 y) / 80% (5 y); deceased 95% / 70%
15 Pancreas: type 1 DM ± renal failure; SPK preferred; bladder drainage → bicarbonate loss → metabolic acidosis
16 Pancreas rejection is hard to detect — biopsy the kidney in SPK as a safer marker
17 MELD = bilirubin + INR + creatinine (± Na); higher = sicker = higher priority (~40 very severe)
18 Liver needs no routine HLA matching, is less immunogenic, and can protect a co-transplanted kidney
19 Hepatic artery thrombosis and primary nonfunction cause early graft failure → urgent retransplantation
20 Piggyback preserves the recipient IVC — essential for living-donor liver grafts; LDLT must be size-compatible

Abdominal Organ Transplantation

Overview of Organ Transplantation

Organ transplantation is a life-saving intervention for patients with end-stage organ failure.

Types of Grafts
  • Autologous: transplanted from one part of the body to another in the same individual.
  • Syngeneic: transplanted between two genetically identical individuals of the same species.
  • Allogeneic: transplanted between two genetically different individuals of the same species.
  • Xenogeneic: transplanted between different species.
Types of Organ Donors
1. Deceased Donor Transplantation (DDT)
Majority (80-90%) of transplants are from deceased donors, classified as:
  • Brain Death Donors (DBD): Organs retrieved after brainstem reflex cessation.
  • Donors after Cardiac Death (DCD): Organs retrieved after circulatory arrest.
Comparison: Brain Death (DBD) vs. Cardiac Death (DCD)
FeatureBrain Death Donor (DBD)Cardiac Death Donor (DCD)
DefinitionIrreversible brainstemDeath after circulatory arrest
loss
Organ ViabilityHigherLower (warm ischemia risk)
KidneyGood functionHigher rate of delayed graft
Transplantfunction
Liver TransplantPreferred5x higher biliary complications
Heart/Lung UseCommonRare
Key Considerations for DCD Donors:
  • Increased ischemic injury (delayed graft function in kidney transplants).
  • Higher rates of biliary complications in liver transplants.
  • New preservation techniques (e.g., normothermic perfusion) improve viability.
2. Living Donor Transplantation (LDT)

Living donation is critical for kidney & liver transplants, offering better graft survival and reduced waitlist time.

Types of Living Donations:
  • Directed donation (to a relative, friend, or designated recipient).
  • Non-directed donation (altruistic) (donor does not specify a recipient).
  • Paired donation (ABO-incompatible donor pairs exchange kidneys for compatibility).
Benefits of Living Donor Transplantation
  • Better long-term graft survival.
  • Lower rejection rates.
  • Shorter waiting time.
  • Elective surgery with planned timing.
  • Lower mortality risk for donors than the general population (due to strict screening).
Risks & Considerations
  • Kidney donors: Slightly increased risk of hypertension & microalbuminuria post-nephrectomy.
  • Liver donors: Higher rates of complications (40%) and perioperative mortality (0.04%).
LDLT (Living Donor Liver Transplantation) Considerations:
  • More common in Asia (due to lower deceased donation rates).
  • Offers survival benefit for MELD > 15 patients, but not for hepatitis C or MELD < 15.
  • Biliary complications (blood supply disruption) are higher in LDLT than in deceased liver transplants.
Organ Allocation & Ethical Considerations
How Organs Are Allocated (UNOS Criteria)

1. Medical urgency (e.g., MELD score for liver transplants). 2. Waitlist duration. 3. Blood type & HLA compatibility. 4. Geographic location (to minimize ischemia time).

5. Organ availability & donor-recipient match.

Ethical Concerns in Organ Transplantation
  • Equal access vs. best outcomes (should the sickest or best-matching patient get priority?).
  • Disparities in wealth & access to transplantation.
  • Use of marginal or high-risk donors (older donors, hepatitis-positive, etc.).

Overview of Transplant Immunology

Organ transplantation introduces foreign antigens into the recipient’s immune system, triggering an alloimmune response that can lead to rejection. This response can be T-cell mediated (cellular rejection) or B-cell mediated (humoral rejection) through preformed antibodies.

Key Components of the Immune Response
  • Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), also known as Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), is the primary determinant of rejection.
  • HLA Classes:
  • Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C): Found on all nucleated cells, recognized by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
  • Class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR): Found on antigen-presenting cells (APCs), recognized by CD4+ helper T cells.
HLA mismatch between donor & recipient determines the severity of immune

response.

Hyperacute rejection is now rare due to pre-transplant compatibility testing (crossmatch & HLA typing).

Alloimmune Responses
Three primary pathways mediate rejection:
1. Direct Allorecognition (Early Rejection)
  • Recipient T cells recognize intact foreign HLA molecules on donor APCs.
  • Rapid & strong response → acute rejection.
2. Indirect Allorecognition (Later Rejection)
  • Donor cells release antigenic peptides, which are processed by recipient APCs.
  • Triggers T-cell activation & antibody production → chronic rejection.
3. Semi-Direct Allorecognition
  • Recipient APCs acquire intact MHC from donor cells.
  • Hybrid process of both direct & indirect pathways.

Blocking these signals is the key mechanism of immunosuppressive drugs.

Antibody-Mediated (Humoral) Rejection (AMR)
  • B cells recognize donor HLA antigens and differentiate into plasma cells, producing donor-specific antibodies (DSAs).
  • DSAs activate:
  • Complement cascade (leading to inflammation & tissue injury).
  • Natural killer (NK) cells & eosinophils.
  • Endothelial dysfunction leading to graft failure.

AMR is more challenging to treat than T-cell-mediated rejection.

Chronic Rejection: The Silent Threat
  • Leading cause of long-term graft failure.
  • Caused by:
  • Ischemia-reperfusion injury.
  • Undetected acute rejection episodes.
  • Fibrosis & vascular damage.
  • Leads to progressive graft dysfunction, often resistant to treatment.
Despite immunosuppression advances, preventing chronic rejection remains a

major challenge.

Immunosuppression in Organ Transplantation

Immunosuppression is crucial in organ transplantation to prevent rejection while minimizing drug toxicity. Therapy typically consists of induction therapy (given at transplantation) and maintenance therapy (long-term post-transplant regimen).

Induction Therapy

Induction therapy provides intense immunosuppression at the time of transplantation to reduce early rejection and allow delayed introduction of nephrotoxic agents (e.g., calcineurin inhibitors).

  • Who benefits? EBV-positive patients to avoid nephrotoxicity.
  • Limitation: Higher rejection rates compared to CNI-based therapy.

Treatment of Acute Rejection in Organ Transplantation

Acute rejection occurs in 8%-9% of kidney transplant recipients within the first year, with higher risks in deceased donor transplants. For liver transplants, rejection rates vary by age, being highest (≥2️0%) in younger patients (1️8-34 years) and decreasing (8%-1️0%) in older patients (≥5️0 years).

Pancreas transplant rejection rates depend on the type of transplant:
  • Simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplant (12.3%)
  • Pancreas transplant alone (16.5%)
  • Pancreas-after-kidney transplant (18.3%)
Treatment of T-Cell Mediated (Acute Cellular) Rejection
  • First-line therapy: High-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone 200- 500 mg for 3+ days).
  • Response rate: 50%-80%
  • If rejection resolves → taper steroids.
  • If rejection persists → move to second-line therapy.
  • Second-line therapy for steroid-resistant rejection:
  • Antithymocyte globulin (ATG) – depletes T cells.
  • Alemtuzumab (anti-CD52) – strong T & B cell depletion.
  • Plasma exchange + IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG) – useful for persistent cases.

Most cases of acute cellular rejection respond to steroids, but severe rejection

may require stronger immunosuppressants.
Treatment of Antibody-Mediated Rejection (AMR)

AMR is one of the major challenges in long-term transplant survival. It is characterized by donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) against HLA antigens and C4d deposition in graft capillaries.

Limitations of Current Immunosuppression

Although immunosuppression has significantly improved transplant survival, there are major limitations:

1. Increased infection risk – particularly for opportunistic infections (CMV, BK

  • virus, fungal infections).

2. Chronic nephrotoxicity – Calcineurin inhibitors (CNI) (Tacrolimus,

  • Cyclosporine) cause kidney damage over time.

3. Cardiovascular & metabolic issues – Hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia

  • are common due to steroids & CNIs.

4. Higher cancer risk – Immunosuppressed patients have a higher incidence of

  • skin cancer, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), and solid
  • tumors.

5. Limited long-term graft survival – Heart and lung transplant survival

  • remains at ~50%-60% at 5 years.
Despite these challenges, immunosuppressive therapy remains the best option
for long-term graft survival.
Future Strategies: Inducing Transplant Tolerance

A major research goal is tolerance induction, where the immune system accepts the transplanted organ without chronic immunosuppression.

Kidney Transplantation

The first successful kidney transplant was performed in 1954 by Dr. Joseph Murray in Boston, marking the beginning of modern organ transplantation. Since then, kidney transplantation has become the preferred treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

Patient Eligibility for Kidney Transplantation
Patients may be listed for a kidney transplant if they have:
  • Advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ≤ 20 mL/min
  • Initiated dialysis (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis)
Absolute Contraindications
Patients with the following conditions are ineligible for transplantation:
  • Active infections (e.g., untreated tuberculosis, HIV with uncontrolled viral load)
  • Active malignancies (except certain low-risk cancers)
  • Substance abuse (alcohol, drugs)
  • Nonadherence to medication
  • Untreated severe psychiatric disorders
Relative Contraindications

These require careful evaluation and individualized decision-making:

  • Severe ischemic heart disease
  • Short life expectancy
  • Advanced age (>65 years, varies by center)
Kidney Allocation System (KAS) & Donor Selection
Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI)
  • A continuous scoring system (0%-100%) that estimates donor kidney longevity
  • Lower KDPI = Better long-term graft survival
  • A KDPI score <20% indicates high-quality kidneys, usually given to patients with long life expectancy
Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) Score
  • A recipient scoring system based on:
  • Age
  • Time on dialysis
  • Diabetes status
  • Previous organ transplant history
Expanded Criteria Donors (ECD) & Donors After Cardiac Death (DCD)
Expanded Criteria Donors (ECD)
  • Older donors (>60 years)
  • Hypertension, diabetes, high-risk behaviors, cardiac death
  • Lower long-term survival but still beneficial for elderly or high-risk recipients
Donors After Cardiac Death (DCD)
  • Organs retrieved after circulatory arrest, leading to prolonged warm ischemia time
  • Higher risk of delayed graft function and primary nonfunction
  • Long-term function comparable to standard deceased donor kidneys

Liver Transplantation

Liver transplantation is a life-saving procedure for patients with end-stage liver disease or acute liver failure. The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is used to prioritize patients based on disease severity.

Indications for Liver Transplantation
Approved Indications
  • Acute hepatic failure (e.g., drug-induced liver injury, viral hepatitis)
  • Cirrhosis with complications (e.g., ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatopulmonary syndrome)
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (most common indication, 18.5% of transplants)
  • Metabolic liver diseases (e.g., hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, glycogen storage diseases)
Absolute Contraindications
  • MELD score <15 (Risks of transplant > Benefits)
  • Severe cardiovascular disease
  • Metastatic cancer or extrahepatic malignancy
  • Active noncompliance or lack of social support

Pancreas Transplantation

Pancreas transplantation is a lifesaving procedure for select patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), particularly type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) with end- stage renal disease (ESRD) or severe metabolic complications. The goal of transplantation is to restore endogenous insulin production, leading to improved glycemic control and quality of life.

Indications for Pancreas Transplantation
Candidates for Pancreas Transplant
Simultaneous Pancreas-Kidney Transplant (SPK):
  • Most common indication for pancreas transplant
  • Patients with T1DM and ESRD
  • Offers both insulin independence and renal replacement
Pancreas After Kidney Transplant (PAK):
  • T1DM patients who have already received a kidney transplant
  • Recommended for patients with persistent metabolic instability despite a kidney transplant
Pancreas Transplant Alone (PTA):
  • Patients with T1DM without ESRD
  • Must have severe metabolic complications, such as:
  • Frequent hypoglycemic unawareness (e.g., seizures, coma, job loss)
  • Labile glucose levels (frequent episodes of ketoacidosis or severe
  • hypoglycemia)
  • Complications from DM (e.g., retinopathy, neuropathy)
Pancreatic Islet Transplantation (Experimental):
  • Donor pancreas is enzymatically digested, and islets are injected into the portal vein
  • Avoids major surgery but has variable insulin independence rates (23%– 90%)
  • Requires multiple donors and long-term immunosuppression
Pancreatic Auto-Islet Transplantation:
  • For patients undergoing total pancreatectomy for refractory chronic pancreatitis
  • Helps preserve some insulin function
Benefits of Pancreas Transplantation
  • Eliminates need for exogenous insulin
  • Restores physiological insulin secretion
  • Prevents diabetic complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy)
  • Improves quality of life and life expectancy
  • Reduces hypoglycemic episodes

SPK Transplantation has the best outcomes, with 5-year patient survival > 85% and graft survival of 70%.
